content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a mechanism, GIP, that prunes gradients by an index perturbation scheme. It selects the top-k significant elements in the gradient and shuffles the indices by the Mallows model, which preserves privacy. Experiments show that the mechanism improves the accuracy of differentially private deep learning by around 1% compared to several other methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

S1. The proposed idea is reasonable under the assumptions in the paper.

S2. Figure 2, Alg. 1, and Alg. 2 clearly describe the proposed solution.

Weaknesses

W1. In the Introduction, the authors list 3 observations but only verify the third one. They should provide more evidence to verify the correctness of the other two.

W2. In Section 4, there is no reference or experiment to support their claim that "most gradients are sparse.

W3. In Definition 3, there seems to be an error: the index sensitivity within S_k should be min{2kd, 2d-2kd}?

W4. Assumption 4 is unrealistic: it assumes that the mean of gradients is exactly 0, which is almost never the case in practice. Without this assumption, the validity of Eq.5 and Eq.7 is unclear.

W5. The paper lists many related and recent works, but omits most of them in the experiments without explaining why. In particular, it omits two states of the art: Tramer & Boneh (2021), and https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.14191, which was published in AAAI 2021.

W6. In the experiments, the author allocate 99% of the privacy budget to perturb indices, and only 1% of the budget to gradient perturbation. This will significantly increases the additive noise for gradient perturbation. It is unclear whether this approach could outperform the state of the art that uses all budgets for gradient perturbation.

W7. The idea of this paper is similar to Wang et al. (2021) in the reference.

content.title: Response to the comments
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer vL8g for giving very professional comments, which greatly help us to improve our paper’s
quality. We have added revision with the revised parts highlighted in blue in the Supplementary Material to facilitate readability. For the points that are recommended for revision, we now explain how these points have been addressed.

Comment 1&2. "In the Introduction ... most gradients are sparse. "

Response 1&2. Thank you for giving a professional comment. We have removed the wrong observation about sparsity and modified observation 1) in Section 1 to "the work  on gradient compression finds that compressions can be done on the gradient with almost no impact on accuracy." Therefore, we explain why the pruning mechanism can effectively reduce the dimensionality of noise in DPSGD from the perspective of gradient compression. We reproduce the experiment of training WRN16-4 on CIFAR10 in [3] and calculate the ratio between the gradient norm and noise norm in each step. The ratio remains around 0.01 during the entire training process.

Comment 3. "In Definition 3,  ... be min{2kd, 2d-2kd}?"

Response 3. This is a typo and we revise it to $\min\\{2kd, 2d-2kd\\}$.

Comment 4. "Assumption 4 is  ... unclear."

Response 4. For in Section 5, we try to enrich the basis for the formulation of Assumption 1. First, we observe that the distribution of the gradients presented becomes increasingly symmetric with a mean of 0 as the number of training epochs increases in the experiments in [1]. Therefore, we assume that the gradients follow a Gaussian distribution with mean 0 to facilitate our analysis of the mechanism. Notably, this assumption could not be fully satisfied in the actual training. Therefore, our selection of the pruning ratio k shows a decreasing trend to reduce the influence of GIP on the gradient in the early training period.

Comment 5. "The paper lists many related ... in AAAI 2021."

Response 5. We conducted an experimental comparison of related work [2][4]. We reproduce the experiments of training with ScatterNet+CNN model on CIFAR10 and compare with GIP at the same $\epsilon$. [2] has better performance at small \epsilon while GIP presents a better performance when $\epsilon \ge 3$, which is consistent with the following statement in [3]: "However, the capacity of this model is limited – only reaching 71% in non-private training ([2]), and thus the more expressive WRN models outperform it whenever $\epsilon \ge 3$."
The work of tempered sigmoid activations ([4]) is also very effective in improving DP-SGD accuracy, and we added a citation and introduction in the Related Work section. We compare the result of CIFAR10 at $\epsilon=7.53$ as reported in [4], where tempered sigmoid [4] achieves 66.2% and GIP achieves 80.39%. We present the result in the Appendix in the revision.

Comment 6. "In the experiments, the author allocate 99% ... for gradient perturbation."
Response 6. This is a typo and we revise the statement to "$\epsilon_2 = 0.01 \epsilon$".

[1] Xiangyi Chen, Steven Z. Wu, and Mingyi Hong. Understanding gradient clipping in private sgd: A geometric perspective. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, pp. 13773–13782, 2020.

[2] Florian Trame`r and Dan Boneh. Differentially private learning needs better features (or much more data). International Conference on Learning Representations, 2021.

[3] Soham De, Leonard Berrada, Jamie Hayes, Samuel L Smith, and Borja Balle. Unlocking high-accuracy differentially private image classification through scale. arXiv preprint arXiv:2204.13650, 2022.

[4] N. Papernot, A. Thakurta, S. Song, S. Chien, and Ú. Erlingsson. Tempered sigmoid activations for deep learning with differential privacy. AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 2021.

[5] Boxin Wang, Fan Wu, Yunhui Long, Luka Rimanic, Ce Zhang, and Bo Li. Datalens: Scalable privacy preserving training via gradient compression and aggregation. In Proceedings of the 2021 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security, pp. 2146–2168, 2021.

[6] Ruixuan Liu, Yang Cao, Masatoshi Yoshikawa, and Hong Chen. Fedsel: Federated sgd under local differential privacy with top-k dimension selection. In International Conference on Database Systems for Advanced Applications, pp. 485–501. Springer, 2020.

[7] Qingqing Ye, Haibo Hu, Xiaofeng Meng, and Huadi Zheng. Privkv: Key-value data collection with local differential privacy. In 2019 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP), pp. 317–331. IEEE, 2019.

content.title: Response to the comments of novelty
content.comment:
Comment 7&8. "The idea of this paper is similar Wang et al. (2021) in the reference. The idea of pruning gradients is not novel ..."

Response 7&8. 
The motivation of GIP method is different from [5]. First, our GIP stems from gradient compression, which reduces the dimensionality by pruning to reduce the noise. In contrast, [5] performs per-example pruning to reduce the sensitivity of the gradient of each example, as presented in the algorithm for applying their scheme on DP-SGD in the appendix. It does not reduce the dimensionality of the noise and keeps adding the same noise to all the gradient dimensions. Second, we present a pruning mechanism different from the common pruning mechanism in SGD [8] used in previous papers ([5-7]). We use Mallows Model to perturb the index to protect the top-k pruning index as no one ever had. In contrast, most of the previous papers are based on random responses for index selection, which cannot guarantee the number of selected gradients, and [5-7] achieves a lower model accuracy compared to GIP.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a gradient index pruning mechanism for DP-SGD, which applies top-$k$ index pruning for the noisy gradient to reduce the error while still guaranteeing privacy. Theoretical proofs about differential privacy as well as empirical benefits of using this mechanism are demonstrated.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper proposes a novel index pruning mechanism and theoretically proves its privacy guarantee. Empirical experiments show a 1-2% accuracy boost using gradient index pruning.

**Weakness:**

1. I suggest still adding citations for $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP, mallows model, basic composition, etc., even though they are well-known to the community. Some formats of citations are also strange, e.g. PrivKVYe et al. (2019) and FedSelLiu et al. (2020) on page 7. I am not sure if it is a typo. Parentheses should be used for SVHN Netzer et al. (2011), ImageNet Deng et al. (2009), etc.

2. Some notations are confusing. In Definition 1, mechanism $K$ but then $M(X)$ in (1). In Definition 2, permutation should not be a subset of $S$. In Definition 3, the index $I$ should not be a subset of $S$. $I$ is used for both the identity matrix in the Gaussian noise and the gradient index. The notations $\odot$ and $M_p(g_t, k)$ are not introduced in Algorithm 2.

3. Could the author explain whether the order of adding noise and pruning matters? The current algorithm first adds a $d$-dimensional Gaussian and then prunes the noised gradient. Will the algorithm that first prunes the gradient and then adds a $(kd)$-dimensional Gaussian work?

4. The paper states the index sensitivity is $\min\\{2kd, d-2kd\\}$ at most. When $k=1/2$, this means the sensitivity is 0. Is there a typo?

5. The privacy budget is $\epsilon_1+T\sum_i\epsilon_2^{(i)}$. When $T$ is large, $\epsilon_2^{(i)}$ and thus $\theta^{(i)}$ in the Mallows model are both very small. The probability distribution $e^{-\theta d}/\Psi$ then tends to the uniform distribution when $\theta\rightarrow 0$. As a result, I expect the top-$k$ pruning behaves similarly to a random sampling on $S_k$ when $T$ is large. Sampling is always a costly task in practice, so simpler algorithms are preferred.

6. The paper shows that the MSE of top-$k$ is small compared to DP-SGD for a special case of Gaussian gradient with zero mean, but it introduces bias through pruning. Convergence rates of DP-SGD can be established. It is not clear whether the theoretical convergence of gradient index pruning can be also proved. The bias may make the algorithm diverge in theory.

7. In Figure 4(a), why does the similarity first increase and then decrease when training proceeds? In Figure 4(b) and (c), why does the accuracy differ (GIP is still better) when the pruning ratio is 1? I expect both random-$k$ and top-$k$ to behave the same when there is no pruning. In Figure 4(d), when $\epsilon_2$ is larger, the performance becomes worse. However, the paper states that $\epsilon_2=0.99\epsilon$ in experiments in Figure 3. Is there a typo?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written. The proposed index pruning mechanism is new.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a novel index pruning mechanism of DP-SGD to reduce noise and shows a 1-2% accuracy boost in experiments.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.title: Response to the comments
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer HoNo for giving very professional comments. Your patient explanations provide much inspiration for our work. We thought that the comments are extremely valuable and greatly help us to improve our paper’s quality and credibility. We have added revision with the revised parts highlighted in blue in the Supplementary Material to facilitate readability. We now explain how these points have been addressed. 

Comment 1. "I suggest still adding ... ImageNet Deng et al. (2009), etc."

Response 1. Thank you for your suggestion. We have added the citations to make the article more rigorous. We have also modified the format of the corresponding citation.

Comment 2. "Some notations are confusing ... in Algorithm 2."

Response 2. We revised the notation mistakes and added the missing definitions of the notations.

Comment 3. "Could the author explain whether ... (kd)-dimensional Gaussian work?"

Response 3. This may be a problem of formulation, where we get the perturbed index on the original gradient and then perform the pruning operation for both the gradient and the noise. We can reduce the multiplication operation of the index by one step by adding noise first and then performing pruning, but the order does not change the final result. Here the two operations $(g+Z)\odot I = g\odot I + Z\odot I $ get the same result.

Comment 4. "The paper states ... Is there a typo?"

Response 4. Yes, we revise it to "$\min \\{2kd, 2d-2kd\\}$".

Comment 5. "The privacy budget is ... so simpler algorithms are preferred."

Response 5. Although $\epsilon_2$ is small, we can find experimentally in Fig. 4(a) that the cosine similarity will be larger in the GIP mechanism, indicating that even though $\epsilon_2$ is small, it still differs from the random sample.

Comment 6. "The paper shows that the MSE ... the algorithm diverge in theory."

Response 6. Although the analysis of convergence is not covered in this paper, we find in the analysis[1] of the convergence of the pruning mechanism that the pruning mechanism still guarantees convergence under certain conditions that the pruning method is a "$\delta$-approximate compressor" as defined in Section 5 in [1]. And GIP will satisfied "k-approximate compressor" which indicates the convergence will be satisfied.

Comment 7. "In Figure 4(a), why does the similarity first increase and then decrease when training proceeds?"

Response 7. We accepted the reviewer's comments and corrected the unclear presentation of the experimental results for the experimental part. The main problems are concentrated in Fig. 4 (b)(c) for the pruning ratio. The misrepresentation here led the reviewer to misunderstand the results in the figure. We added our choice of experimental parameters for k as {0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 0.7} and highlighted k=0.7 in the figure. In the beginning, clipping perturbation is large, so cosine similarity is low. As the training proceeds, part of the gradient decreases, influence from clipping reduces and the cosine similarity improves. Finally, due to the continuous accumulation of noise, the proportion of noise relative to the gradient increases, and the cosine similarity decreases.


[1] S. U. Stich, S. P. Karimireddy, The Error-Feedback Framework: Better Rates for SGD with Delayed Gradients and Compressed Updates, Journal of Machine Learning Research, 21 (2020) 1-36

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a new method to reduce the dimension of gradients in DP-SGD. Specifically, only the components in the gradient whose weight is greater than some quantile is preserved and then a randomization is applied to get the final index set.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The authors aim to reduce the dimensionality of the gradients in DP-SGD to reduce the noise norm, improves the cosine similarity between the non-private and private gradients and thus improves the utility of DP-SGD. The advantage of the propose method, GIP, over previous dimension reduction approach for DP-SGD is that it can be used in a standalone manner without requiring public data.

To preserve the privacy of the dimension reduction phase, the authors draw the index matrices from a randomized distribution to achieve DP.

The experiment results surprisingly show that GIP can improve the accuracy of DP-SGD compared with full gradient training.

Weakness:  
The computation complexity of the index matrix randomization is high. Could the authors provide a detailed discussion of the computation complexity?

Although ImageNet is hard, De et al. still achieves over 30% accuracy when $\epsilon=8$. The results in Table 1 only report the results in the very first few steps of the training. It will be helpful to show the comparison at more reasonable $\epsilon$ values like 8.

content.comment:
We thank Reviewer MATw for the valuable comments. We have added revision with the revised parts highlighted in blue in the Supplementary Material to facilitate readability. We now explain how the comments have been addressed.

Comment 1. "The computation complexity of the index matrix randomization is high. Could the authors provide a detailed discussion of the computation complexity?"

Response 1. The feasible domain of our index random variables is a finite discrete space $S_k$. Compared to the Mallows model, which is defined on all possible d-dimensional permutations, our feasible domain is a subset of theirs, which greatly reduces the sampling overhead.

We present the index perturbation algorithm in Appendix A.2, in which we first sample a changing length as a random variable, and turn the digit of 0s into 1s and 1s into 0s by the previously sampled length. Compared to the per-example clip, the computational overhead of index perturbation is mild, as the difference in training time is given in Table 2.

Comment 2. "Although ImageNet is hard, ... values like 8."

Response 2. Thanks. Due to the limitation of computational resources, we will deliver the full results of ImageNet in the next version of revision.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a noisy gradient method that attempts to solve the issue of low signal-to-noise ratio of DPSGD when the gradients are sparse. This is done by taking the top-k components of the gradient (where k is a hyper-parameter), then decoupling the protection of the gradient's support (referred to as index), and its values.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
The main technical contribution is the use of the Mallows distribution to protect the top-k indices, and to prove the corresponding privacy guarantee. The idea of using the Mallows model in this context is new, and the experimental results seem promising with significant improvements on some benchmarks in the small epsilon regime.

## Weaknesses
My main concern is with the theoretical analysis. The authors claim that the analysis proves their method uses less noise compared to DPSGD. But I have serious doubts about the relevance of the result.

First, the statement itself (Corollary 1) does not quantify the improvement, it only gives a condition under which there is a non-zero improvement in the approximation error. There is no discussion of the effect of important parameters such as dimension or sparsity.

Second, the analysis is done under some strong assumptions and approximations:
- The gradients are assumed to be normally distributed (Assumption 1), which leads to non-sparse gradients, while the motivation is to address sparse gradients. So there is a mismatch between the motivation and analysis. The fact that sparsity is not even modeled is concerning.
- The analysis does not seem to take clipping into account, since the MSE (equation 5) is defined as the difference between the noisy *unclipped* gradient and the exact gradient.

The empirical results are certainly more compelling than the analysis. But they also leave many important questions unanswered. In particular, there is no discussion about the effect of gradient sparsity or the choice of the parameter k.
- How sparse are the models under consideration, and how does the sparsity affect the performance of the method?
- Why is the decay of the pruning ratio k necessary?
- Is the default clipping value of 1 a reasonable hyper-parameter choice (did the authors attempt to tune it)?
- In which settings is this method relevant, and when should one expect improvement? For instance, sparsity of gradients can be very different for different classes of models.

Figure 1: although the experiment shows a clear tend, it's unclear how this relates to the proposed method. First, the work seeks to solve the problem of sparse gradients, but the experiment uses gradients sampled from a normal distribution. Second, the figure only shows the DPSGD gradient perturbation, did the authors try the same experiment with their method?

The experiment in Figure 4-(b,c) require some further explanation. Shouldn't the performance of random-k and GIP (as well as DPSGD) be similar when k tends to 1? In this case there is no pruning and all methods should have a similar performance. This does not seem to be the case on the figures, as the gap persists even when k is close to 1.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Some issues to be addressed:
- It is claimed in the introduction that pre-training does not show promising results in other areas such as computer vision, but this is not true. See for example [1,2]
- At the beginning of Section 4, the paper claims "... the fact that most gradients are sparse ...". This is presented as a fact, without references or arguments to support this claim. Not all models have sparse gradients. Typically, models with large embedding layers (input or output layers) have highly sparse gradients.
- Some notation is used without definition, for example $g(W, x)$ at the beginning of Section 3.
- Avoid overloaded notation. For example the symbol $g$ is used both for the sum of gradients, and for individual terms in the sum.
- At the beginning of Section 4, it is claimed that the perturbation error of DPSGD grows linearly with the dimension. This should either say the *squared* error grows linearly, or the error grows as the square root of the dimension.
- In the introduction, it is mentioned that "few works have discussed the impact of gradient sizes", but it's unclear what this refers to. In particular, many works discuss dependence on the dimension, and some works have also explore the effect of sparsity.
- $\Phi$ in Proposition 2 is undefined (it seems to be define much later in the appendix).
- In Section 6.1, did the authors mean $\epsilon_2 = 0.01 \epsilon$ (instead of 0.99)?

[1] De et al., Unlocking High-Accuracy Differentially Private Image Classification through Scale.
[2] Tramèr & Boneh, Differentially private learning needs better features (or much more data). ICLR 2021
content.summary_of_the_review: Novel idea, with a weak theoretical analysis, but promising experimental results. Expanded experiments, and more discussion of the effects of sparsity, can make this a solid empirical paper.

content.title: Response to the comments
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer 4SuY for the valuable comments. Your comments have helped us improve the article. We have added revision with the revised parts highlighted in blue in the Supplementary Material to facilitate readability. We now explain how each point has been addressed.

Comment 1. "First, the statement itself (Corollary 1) ... dimension or sparsity."

Response 1. We give the values of beta with respect to dimensionality and pruning ratio in Appendix B.1. And beta increases with k or d.

Comment 2. "The gradients are assumed ... modeled is concerning."

Response 2. We have removed the wrong statement about sparsity and modified observation 1) in Section 1 to "the work [1] on gradient compression finds that compression can be done on gradients with almost no impact on accuracy in SGD." 

Comment 3. "The analysis does not seem ... the exact gradient."

Response 3. Thank you for the comment. We add the analysis for clipping, according to the discussion in [2]: "Theorem 2 states that when the noise distribution is symmetric, gradient clipping will keep the expected clipped gradients positively aligned with the true gradient. This is the desired property that can guarantee convergence." In the case of Assumption 1, the symmetric gradient distribution causes less perturbation to the gradient in the clipping mechanism. Therefore, in the analysis of MSE, we only analyze the impact generated by the pruning mechanism and noise. The impact of clipping on the DP-SGD is out of the scope of this paper. 

In Section 5, we reaffirm the supporting evidence for Assumption 1. We observe that the distribution of the gradients shows a symmetric distribution centered at 0 as the number of training epochs increases in the experiments in [2]. Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that the gradients follow a Gaussian distribution with 0 mean. 

Comment 4. "The empirical results are ... the performance of the method?"

Response 4. We corrected the statement on gradient sparsity (see response 2). The impact of different pruning ratios is given in Fig. 4 (b)(c).

Comment 5. "Why is the decay of ... different classes of models."

Response 5. This is because the gradients typically vary a great deal at the beginning of the training. Hence we kept most of the gradients at the start.

We fix clipping value to 1 in all experiments in accord with the settings of [3]. Here we also provide evidence from [4] that the hyperparameter selection of DP-SGD can be done without adjusting the clipping value, and small clipping threshold works better.

Comment 6. "Figure 1: ... try the same experiment with their method?"

Response 6. Fig. 1 is meant to say the trend of cosine similarity increases with the dimensionality. We compared the cosine similarity of Jax-privacy, Random-k, and our GIP methods in Fig. 4(a).

Comment 7. "The experiment in Figure 4-(b,c) ... when k is close to 1."

Response 7. The performance of random-k and GIP (as well as DPSGD) are indeed closer when k tends to 1. But the figure does not show the results when k is close to 1. We highlighted the choice of k as {0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 0.7} in the figure.  The misrepresentation here led to the confusion of the results. 

Comment 8. "It is claimed in the introduction ... and for individual terms in the sum."

Response 8. Thank you for the comment. In the revision, we have rectified the notations.

Comment 9. "At the beginning of Section 4 ... square root of the dimension."

Response 9. At the beginning of Section 4, we claimed that $E_z||M(\bar{g}) - \bar{g}||_2^2 = \sigma^2 C^2 d$, clearly showing the error grows linearly with the dimension d.

Comment 10. "In the introduction, it is mentioned ... explore the effect of sparsity."

Response 10. We have added references to related work and also included work [5].

Comment 11. "$\Phi$ in Proposition 2 is undefined ... did the authors mean $\epsilon_2 = 0.01 \epsilon$(instead of 0.99)?"

Response 11. We added the definition and revised the statement to "$\epsilon_2 = 0.01 \epsilon$".

[3] Soham De, Leonard Berrada, Jamie Hayes, Samuel L Smith, and Borja Balle. Unlocking high-accuracy differentially private image classification through scale. arXiv preprint arXiv:2204.13650, 2022.

[4] Zhiqi Bu,Yu-Xiang Wang,Sheng Zha,George Karypis. Automatic Clipping: Differentially Private Deep Learning Made Easier and Stronger. arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.07136, 2022

content.title: Re: Response to the comments
content.comment:
Thank you for the corrections made to the paper, and the additional references. The updates have improved the paper, though many of the original concerns remain unaddressed.

There is an important change in the motivation of the paper in the revision. The paper was originally motivated by the problem of sparse gradients, while the revision talks about gradient compression. The connection with compression is not explored, and this point should be discussed more carefully given that it's used as motivation.

Regarding the analysis:
- Thank you for pointing to the dependence of $\beta$ on problem parameters. It is still the case, however, that Corollary 1 does not quantify the improvement, it only gives conditions under which there is an improvement.
- The Gaussian gradients assumption should be acknowledged as a very strong assumption, even if empirically, the gradients have zero mean.
- Thank you for confirming that clipping is not handled in the analysis.

Regarding experiments:
- My question about Fig. 1 remains unanswered. It is unclear why the proposed method was not tried on the same (synthetic) experiment.
- Clipping value of 1: the authors refer to [4] that 

>the hyperparameter selection of DP-SGD can be done without adjusting the clipping value

Are the authors using the clipping method described in [4]? Notice that this is not the same as standard clipping. In fact, the authors of [4] state that for standard clipping, "the choice of clipping norm R, however, is shown to be vital for achieving high accuracy under DP". If the authors are indeed using the clipping method of [4], this should be clarified.

content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method to privately select the top-k coordinates of the gradient for DPSGD, so that the utility can be improved.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The problem of extracting useful information from the noisy gradient in DPSGD is an important problem.

Weakness:
The privacy analysis is not clear to me.
- It's not quite clear to me why the sensitivity of the top-k index is min{2kd, d-2kd}. For example, if k = 0.5, by changing one example, the non-zero index can change from the first half to the latter half, giving a sensitivity of d. (Not to mention that the min would be negative if k > 0.5.)
- Proposition 1 says Algorithm 2 would guarantee (epsilon_1, delta)-DP. Should the privacy contain both epsilon_1 + epsilon_2 instead (as is in Theorem 2)?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The privacy analysis might need more clarification.
Another question: the NNs in the experiments do not have batch normalization (which might cause privacy issue), right?

Quality:
The privacy analysis is not quite clear to me (see section above). This is an important part of the paper and I might need further clarification from the authors to judge the quality.

Novelty:
I think there are some previous work on trying to extract useful information from noisy gradient. For example, https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01294. You might need to do a more throughout search of past work.

One other comment:
The experiments allocate most of the privacy budget to the index perturbation with epsilon_2 = 0.99*epsilon, which is a bit surprising to me. With only 1% budget allocated for the gradient clipping and noising, it is hard for me to imagine the final gradient being meaningful. Can you elaborate more on the reasoning behind the allocation?
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem is interesting and important, but the privacy analysis is a bit unclear to me.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to the comments
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer 8TyJ for the valuable comments, which greatly helps us improve our paper. We have added revision with the revised parts highlighted in blue in the Supplementary Material to facilitate readability.
The following is the explanation to each comment.

Comment 1. "It's not quite clear to ... be negative if k > 0.5."

Response 1. We have corrected typos mentioned, including 1) the definition of index sensitivity modified to "$\min \\{2kd, 2d-2kd \\}$" in Section 4; 2) the statement of the privacy budget for index perturbation is modified to "$\epsilon_2 = 0.01 \epsilon$" in Section 6.

Comment 2. "Proposition 1 says ... (as is in Theorem 2)?"

Response 2. Proposition 1 says Algorithm 2 with random-k pruning would guarantee $(\\epsilon_1, \delta)$-DP. No additional privacy budget is incurred in the index selection procedure in random-k, which is different from top-k.

Comment 3. "Novelty: I think there are ... search of past work."

Response 3. Thank you for the comment. We add [1] in related work and compare with GIP method. As we state in the paper, [1] is based on the property of gradient sparsity in NLP tasks, but the property may not hold in other tasks, such as computer vision ones.

Comment 4. "The experiments allocate most ... behind the allocation?"

Response 4. Please see Response 1.


[1] Huanyu Zhang, Ilya Mironov, and Meisam Hejazinia. Wide network learning with differential privacy. CoRR, abs/2103.01294, 2021.
